observation_summary: The compiler fails to issue warnings for side-effect-free expressions when they appear in non-rightmost positions within a comma-separated expression sequence. The test case expects a warning for useless code, but the compiler reports zero warnings.
hypothesis: The side-effect checking logic for comma-separated expressions is incomplete. It only evaluates the first element of the sequence for side effects, ignoring subsequent non-rightmost elements that also lack side effects.
prediction: The code responsible for traversing comma expressions will be updated to iterate through all elements except the rightmost one, checking each for side effects instead of just the first one.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly states that only the first element is checked. The failing test confirms that useless code in non-rightmost positions (e.g., '2' in '(bar(), 2, 42)') does not trigger the expected warning. This is a procedural logic error in the side-effect analysis algorithm.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a failure to correctly implement the side-effect analysis algorithm for comma operators. It is not a missing guard (Checking) because the logic exists but is insufficient; it is not an assignment error; it is a procedural flaw in how the compiler traverses and validates expression sequences.
evidence_used: Bug report description: 'When it comes to an expression involving the comma operator, only the first element of such a sequence is checked for being free of side effects.'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While a check is missing for non-rightmost elements, the root cause is the algorithmic strategy of only checking the first element, rather than a simple missing guard on a single variable or condition.
